Its cutoff of 3 partitions regional agrosilvopastoral aptitude versus conservation priority; it is not a land-cover category or an independent soil/slope threshold. quote:
Costa et al. (2019) divided the PCU into five classes regarding the 
potential for conservation use. This work adopted the most straightfor­
ward division for analysing the fitness for use: PCU ≥3 indicated apti­
tude for agrosilvopastoral activities and PCU<3 for biodiversity 
conservation (Table 2). The methodology allows rapid reprocessing 
allowing different divisions readily. Although, we do not ignore the need 
for conservation initiatives inside the productive landscape to ensure 
adequate supplies of pollinators, seed dispersers, herbivores, natural 
enemies, and so on (Nelson and Burchfield, 2021). Moreover, it is also 
necessary to consider conserving the streamflow margins and other 
areas demanded by law (Brazil, 2021).

quote: The paucity of the soil seed bank of the ﬂoodplain after decades of human occupation and limited dispersal of desirable species are widely seen as the main con-straints for the recovery of the plant community in European meadows and U.S. swamps (articles 9, 39, 41, 65 and 139 Appendix S1).
raw_name: paucity of floodplain soil seed bank + limited propagule dispersal
attribution: synthesis of articles 9, 39, 41, 65 and 139 of the review's Appendix S1
selection_justification: This is THE dominant limiting factor of the natural_restored family made explicit: whether a degraded riparian site can regenerate without planting depends on residual seed bank and propagule supply, both degraded by prolonged prior agricultural use. It generalises across two continents and many studies (not n=1 site context), and is a suitability/applicability statement rather than an effectiveness result. VONT GAP flagged: no canonical variable yet exists for regeneration potential in riparian systems (the FMNR analogue `rootstock_presence` is NOT interchangeable - seed bank and living rootstock are different mechanisms), so a descriptive id is used and raised for the team. FAMILY NOTE: the claim is generic-riparian (it applies to retained/regenerated and to planted buffers alike); no riparian cross_family id exists, so it is filed under the family the source was discovered and screened under (riparian_buffer__natural_restored), per the 2026-09 sweep brief.

relationship.measured_as: statutory minimum riparian reserve width on EACH side of the watercourse
relationship.direction: required riparian reserve width increases with watercourse width

context.instrument: Native Vegetation Protection Law, Federal Law No. 12,651/2012

quote: In Brazil, the Native Vegetation Protection Law (Federal Law Number 12,651/2012) states that landowners in all biomes must protect a minimum width of ripar-ian reserves. The extent of these riparian reserves varies according to watercourse width (e.g. from 30 m on each side for watercourses up to 10-m wide to 500-m for watercourses larger than 600-m width).

attribution: Brazilian Native Vegetation Protection Law, Federal Law No. 12,651/2012 (as reported by Dala-Corte et al. 2020)
selection_justification: Hard legal mask material, which the 2026-06-23 routing keeps INSIDE T4 (only soft, investment-addressable enabling-environment factors go to M2b). The statutory ladder is directly mappable: a distance raster from the stream network, keyed to watercourse width class. Only the two endpoints stated verbatim in the quote are encoded; the intermediate statutory classes are not in this source and are NOT invented. This is a national normative rule, not the study's own site context.

relationship.direction: watercourse size class is the gating variable that selects which riparian reserve width applies

relationship.measured_as: riparian reserve width on EACH side of the stream channel
relationship.direction: reserves narrower than the stated width are insufficient; wider reserves give additional benefit

context.evidence_base: TITAN thresholds over 1,149 fish and 1,449 aquatic-invertebrate stream sites
context.watercourses: small streams up to 10 m wide

quote: Therefore, maintaining 50 m of ripar-ian reserves on each side of the stream channel (resulting in a 100-m wide strip in total) would most effectively avoid crossing thresholds of aquatic biodiversity loss in Brazil.
raw_name: science-based recommended minimum riparian reserve width per side
selection_justification: Extracted as T4 because the authors state it as a SITING/DESIGN REQUIREMENT ('maintaining 50 m of riparian reserves on each side'), which the sweep brief permits for biodiversity width thresholds; the underlying biodiversity DOSE-RESPONSE results (mean thresholds of 6.5% / 2.9% native-vegetation loss, and the per-biome threshold tables) are outcome responses = deferred nbs_effect and are deliberately NOT extracted and NOT relabelled. claim_basis=modelled because the recommendation is derived from the paper's TITAN threshold models. NOTE for synthesis: this science-based minimum is ~1.7x the federal statutory minimum for the same stream class (see ev_distance_to_waterbody_dalacorte20_1) - a genuine, documented divergence.

relationship.direction: sub-national regulations set riparian reserve widths above the federal minimum and scale them with watercourse size

context.municipalities: Bonito (Mato Grosso do Sul); Aparecida de Goiania (Goias)

quote: For example, the city of Bonito (Mato Grosso do Sul State), which relies on ecotourism, has a specific regulation that mandates the protection of 50-m wide riparian reserves around watercourses of rural areas (Bonito, 2004). Aparecida de Goiânia (Goiás State) has also a specific municipal regulation of 50-m wide riparian reserves for small watercourses, and 100 m for other larger rivers (Aparecida de Goiânia, 2018).

attribution: Bonito (2004) municipal law, Mato Grosso do Sul; Aparecida de Goiania (2018) Lei Complementar No. 152, Goias
selection_justification: Worked example of a CONTEXT OVERRIDE for the T4 binding layer: sub-national statutes set riparian widths above the national floor and key them to watercourse size, which is exactly the most-specific-context-wins pattern the recipe encodes via `context_overrides`. Hard legal mask material, so it stays in T4.

quote: The high variability in biodiversity responses to loss of native riparian vegetation suggests caution in the use of a single riparian width for conservation actions or policy definitions nationwide.
raw_name: caution against a single national riparian width
selection_justification: Variable-selection / parameterisation evidence, deliberately carrying NO relationship: it does not set a width, it establishes that a SINGLE global width is not defensible and that riparian width must be context-resolved. Directly supports emitting the T4 riparian-width row with `context_overrides` plus an honest uncertainty band rather than one global number.

quote: In addition, for riparian reserves cleared before 2008, the law allows agricultural activities within them and states that restoration depends on property size (Brancalion et al., 2016). As a consequence, riparian reserves are even smaller in private properties where deforestation occurred before 2008, and watercourse width is not taken into consid-eration in these cases.

attribution: Brancalion et al. (2016); Brazilian Native Vegetation Protection Law
selection_justification: Enabling-environment / compliance caveat -> operational_risk (M2b Stream-B), not T4. Materially qualifies the T4 statutory mask extracted from the same page: the legally protected riparian width is NOT uniform, because pre-2008 clearing triggers a property-size-dependent derogation in which watercourse width is ignored. Flagged so the mask is not applied more strictly than the law actually binds. No numeric rule is encoded (the derogation's property-size bands are not in this source).

context.instruments: PES, concessional credit, rural land-tax relief

quote: Creating and expanding economic incentives for landowners that protect large riparian reserves can be more effective than tradi-tional command-and-control approaches. Economic incentives may include payment for ecosystem services, access to lower interest rate loans and reduced rural territorial taxes.
raw_name: economic incentives for landowners protecting riparian reserves (PES, lower-interest loans, reduced rural land taxes)
selection_justification: Soft, investment-addressable enabling-environment lever -> operational_risk (M2b Stream-B) and Module-6 next-steps. Relevant because riparian reserves sit on private land (the source notes ~62% of Brazil is privately owned), so finance instruments, not the mask alone, determine whether restoration happens. No threshold, hence scoping_candidate with a null relationship.

relationship.measured_as: riparian zone (Permanent Preservation Area) buffer width measured from the river network
relationship.direction: the riparian zone is delineated as a fixed-width band from the river network, with a wider radial buffer around springs

context.instrument: Native Vegetation Protection Law of Brazil (Brasil, 2012) — Permanent Preservation Area (PPA/APP)
context.corroboration: FAO recommendation and Welsch (1991) give the same 30 m

quote: We adopted the Permanent Preservation Area (PPA) that is deﬁned by the Native Vegetation Protection Law of Brazil (Brasil, 2012) as a riparian zone. We have adopted partially the law and used a 30 m-buﬀer along the river network and a 50 m buﬀer around springs. We did not consider special cases of the law that allow reducing the PPA to only 5 m. FAO recommendation for riparian zone to water quality protection is also 30 m, as well as proposed by Welsch (1991).
raw_name: Permanent Preservation Area (PPA) riparian zone delineation: 30 m river buffer, 50 m spring buffer, 5 m reduced statutory case
observed_dataset: IBGE 1:50,000 stream network + 5 m DEM-derived river network, ArcGIS 10.2
attribution: Native Vegetation Protection Law of Brazil (Brasil, 2012); FAO; Welsch (1991)
selection_justification: The single most directly usable riparian T4 mask rule in this sweep: it gives the statutory delineation geometry (fixed-width band from the river network PLUS a distinct radial buffer around SPRINGS/headwater sources, a spatial feature no other source in the sweep supplies), the reduced statutory case, and an independent FAO corroboration of the same 30 m - all in one contiguous quote. Extracted from a methods section (a section type the catalogue warns about) ONLY because the content is a national statutory + FAO normative rule that generalises, not the study site's own measured conditions; it is therefore not site_context. Encoded as a delineation rule; the paper's water-quality results are deferred nbs_effect and are not extracted.

relationship.direction: published riparian-zone delineation widths span well above the national statutory minimum, and the delineation width chosen changes which scale appears to control the system

context.studies: Tran et al. (2010), USA; Shen et al. (2015), China

attribution: Tran et al. (2010); Shen et al. (2015)
selection_justification: Emitted as scoping_candidate, not a threshold: it records the RANGE of riparian-zone delineation widths in use (100-200 m) and the methodological finding that the chosen width determines whether riparian- or watershed-scale land cover appears dominant. Useful as an uncertainty/ sensitivity input to the T4 riparian-width row, not as a suitability bound - hence no abs_/opt_ keys.

quote: Low-order streams (1st to 3rd orders) dominate a riverine land-scape, and they contribute to the function, health, and biodiversity of the entire river networks (Vannote et al., 1980; Wipﬂi et al., 2007). Terrestrial inputs strongly inﬂuence low-order streams (Vannote et al., 1980), which make them fragile ecosystems that can suﬀer dramatic impacts of land-use changes.

attribution: Vannote et al. (1980); Wipfli et al. (2007)
selection_justification: Variable-selection evidence for stream_order as a riparian targeting variable: low-order streams dominate the network and are the most strongly influenced by adjacent terrestrial inputs, so they are where riparian condition matters most. Deliberately emitted WITHOUT shape params: the source defines the low-order class (1st-3rd) but does NOT state a targeting rule of the form 'buffer orders 1-3', and encoding abs_min/abs_max here would be the extractor's inference, not the source's claim.

relationship.direction: low-productivity pasture with low stocking adjacent to watercourses is the preferred land-cover class for riparian forest restoration (low opportunity cost, high restorable area)

raw_name: low-productivity pastureland as the restoration opportunity class
attribution: Latawiec et al. (2015)
selection_justification: System-constraint targeting rule on adjacent land cover: it names the mappable land-cover class where riparian restoration is most feasible in tropical agricultural landscapes, which is the 'constrain by observed distribution' logic applied to the host land-use system. Generalising (stated for tropical agricultural landscapes), not a site observation. No threshold is stated, so `relationship` carries direction and the target class only - no invented scale.

relationship.direction: buffer width requirement is conditioned on slope: on gentle slopes below the stated gradient the stated width range is adequate; steeper ground requires wider buffers

context.context: agricultural riparian buffer strips, diffuse-pollution mitigation

quote: This makes it difficult to derive generic optimum widths, however, for gentle slopes (less than 10 % gradient), widths of 8–15 m are typically adequate (Dorioz et al., 2006).
raw_name: slope gradient (%) as the conditioning factor for adequate buffer strip width
attribution: Dorioz et al. (2006)
justification_quote: Optimum width depends on site-specific factors (e.g. run-off sediment loads, pollutant type, soil type and slope), vegetation structure (influencing the ability of the vegetation to trap sediments and sediment bound pollutants) and spe-cies composition (influencing assimilation and biodegradation) (Dosskey et al., 2008, 2010; Schmitt et al., 1999).
selection_justification: The only quantified slope rule recovered in this sweep, and the cleanest slope->width design relationship: it conditions the required riparian strip width on slope gradient. Deliberately NOT encoded with abs_min/abs_max on slope - the 10% figure is the BREAKPOINT at which the stated width range ceases to be adequate, NOT a hard slope exclusion, and reading it as one would be the lowest-rank-class-as-exclusion defect. FAMILY: assigned to riparian_buffer__planted because the claim is explicitly about deliberately established vegetated/grass buffer strips in agricultural fields, not about retained or naturally regenerating riparian vegetation.

relationship.direction: a wider riparian strip is required where soluble pollutants (nitrates, dissolved phosphorus) rather than sediment-bound pollutants are the design target

quote: Schmitt et al. (1999) suggested widths of 7.5 m are ef-fective at trapping sediments and sediment-bound pollutants (e.g. non-soluble phosphates), whereas to control soluble pollutants (e.g. nitrates and dissolved phosphorus) widths of 15 m are recommended.

attribution: Schmitt et al. (1999)
justification_quote: Optimum width depends on site-specific factors (e.g. run-off sediment loads, pollutant type, soil type and slope), vegetation structure (influencing the ability of the vegetation to trap sediments and sediment bound pollutants) and spe-cies composition (influencing assimilation and biodegradation) (Dosskey et al., 2008, 2010; Schmitt et al., 1999).

Water availability is a critical factor in selecting wetland location. The distance
from frequently flowing streams has a strong influence on the total cost of the
wetland restoration or creation project. Very suitable areas were considered those
within ∼500 m from a frequently flowing stream. Long distances imply high energy
requirements and financial expenditures. Buffers of one hundred and fifty meters
radius were considered as the spatial units that noticeably increase energy and
economical costs. We considered unsuitable for wetland mitigation all catchment
areas located above the highest point where water flowed frequently. In these areas,
only water pumping could keep water on the wet

In this study, adjustments were made to the definitions of target 
areas for afforestation and reforestation based on the regulations set by 
the UNFCCC and Ministry of Forestry (MoFE 2015). Afforested areas 
were defined as non-forested regions of > 50 years. However, owing to 
data limitations, an adjusted approach was adopted in which the target 
areas for afforestation were identified by integrating non-forested 
regional information defined as of 2000. This information was sourced 
from Global Forest Watch data (Hansen et al., 2013), integrated with 
impervious surface data from 1983 to 2000 (Gong et al., 2020), and 
MODIS land-cover data since 2000 (USGS, 2010). Consequently, the 
targeted reforestation areas in this study focused on regions with low 
forest cover or non-forested areas observed from 2000 to 2023.

relationship.direction: tied ridging performs best on coarser-textured soils in the semi-arid site; on clay (fine-textured) soils ridge tillage can induce waterlogging followed by mass movement and erosion - a negative on heavy clays

quote:
The best CEM techniques were diﬀerent for both sites. In Mbeere
South, tied ridging was the best followed by mulching practice while in
Meru South mulching was the best. The tied ridges in the semi-arid site
were hardly destroyed during the cropping season leading to increased
water content in the soil proﬁle and good crop performance while in the
sub-humid site the ridges were repaired often. On clay soils (in Meru
South), ridge tillage can induce water logging, and later on followed by
mass movement/soil erosion (FAO, 1993). Mulching retained more soil
water content in Meru South since the region received more rainfall
compared with Mbeere South. In addition, soils in Meru South are ﬁne
textured, clay while Mbeere South the soils are coarser. Reduced soil
water retention is observed in coarse textured (Mbeere South) than in
ﬁne-textured soils

quote: Meskat is rectangular shaped runoff basin. It consists of a catchment area called meskat of about 500 m² in size, and a cropping area called mankaa of about 250 m² (C:A ratio of 2:1). quote: Out of seven studies conducted on erosion control, 49 observa- tions were identified for runoff and 49 for soil loss. The studies were conducted in Kenya, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe. Our findings show that agroforestry performed best in terms of erosion reduc- tion ecosystem services, five and ten times better than controls for runoff (RR: 5.0; 95% CI: 3.3-7.9) and soil loss (RR: 9.7; 95% CI: 5.9-17.3). However, these very large effect sizes could also be due to publication bias as demonstrated by the high Kendall’s rank correlation coefficients. If we had found more published studies (larger sample sizes), we expect the effect sizes to be more modest than the figures we reported here. Erosion control with agroforestry was more effective in both humid (RR 7.2; 95% CI 4.8 to 13.9) and semi-arid zones (RR 8.0; 95% CI 4.8 to 16.7) compared to controls. Similarly, erosion control with agroforestry was more effective when either shrubs (RR 6.9; 95% CI 4.6 to 11.4) or trees (RR 11.1; 95% CI 6.1 to 24.7) were planted.

relationship.direction_cue: stock an average of 24.2 ± 2.8 Mg C ha−1

context.note: Pooled mean +/- SE (2.8). Systematic review of 185 East-African publications (livelihoods n = 152, carbon n = 43). NOTE: these are carbon STOCKS (Mg C per ha), not sequestration RATES — a rate requires a time denominator the review does not give.

quote: This review shows that agroforestry systems in East Africa stock an average of 24.2 ± 2.8 Mg C ha−1 in biomass and 98.8 ± 12.2 Mg C ha−1 in the soil (Fig. 3). The combined estimate of carbon in biomass and the soil is larger than what was estimated to be the potential carbon storage (29–53 Mg C ha−1) of agrosilvicultural systems in the humid tropics of Africa (Albrecht and Kandji, 2003), but lower than systems with high stem density, large mean tree size, and longer maximum ages i.e. over 60 years reported in Southeast Asia (Roshetko et al., 2007). The difference with earlier estimates is mostly in the soil part where several method­ ological issues need to be considered (Hairiah et al., 2020), such as variation in the soil depth included and changes in soil bulk density that influence which soil is included in a fixed-depth sample (Schrumpf et al., 2011). The amount varies depending on agroforestry practice, ranging from 26.7 ± 7.0 Mg C ha−1 in improved fallows to 153±23 Mg C ha−1 in homegardens.

Market-oriented agroforestry interventions (for example, Acacia decurrens) that 
bring sustainable income for smallholders can be vital ingredients in creating incentives 
for the adoption of biological measures for land restoration and improving resilience to 
climate shocks. Agroforestry systems, such as Acacia decurrens, that bring additional 
benefits through nitrogen fixation while also generating cash income are vital win-win 
options for land restoration, income growth, and asset creation. The lesson is that in the 
microwatersheds where such market-oriented agroforestry practices have been 
supported (for example, Akusty in Fagita Lekoma, Amhara), this has induced 
transformational changes in restoring highly degraded landscapes, creating 
employment, generating income, and reducing poverty and out-migration.

72. Contribution to climate resilience. Results of a World Bank study suggest that well-established SPS could help 
reduce vulnerability to climate shocks.47 While extensive CR operations in Colombia reported milk productivity losses 
of up to 19 percent during periods of climate variability from 2009 to 2019, farms with well-established SPS reported 
productivity losses of just 0.4-5.5 percent. Under a scenario where SPS are implemented at scale, projections suggest

improved vegetative cover and efficient land management reduce vulnerability.

quote: Dès les premières pluies, ils disposent de 100 à 500 m3 d'eau de ruissellement assez chargée, soit pour irriguer un petit jardin qui, bien fumé et irrigué à la raie et au zaï peut produire deux cultures : maïs précoce de soudure et pastèques tardives. Elles peuvent aussi servir à alimenter en eau le bétail qui perdra moins de poids en fin de saison sèche s'il n'a pas à se déplacer jusqu'au point d'eau dans la vallée. Cet aménagement qui améliore surtout la sécurité alimentaire à l'époque de la soudure (English: From the first rains, they have 100 to 500 m3 of rather loaded runoff water, either to irrigate a small garden which, well manured and furrow- and zai-irrigated, can produce two crops: early lean-season maize and late watermelons. They can also be used to water livestock, which will lose less weight at the end of the dry season if it does not have to travel to the water point in the valley. This treatment, which above all improves food security at the lean season)

relationship.outcome_raw: domestic rooftop cisterns judged to give households basic water access (under one km, under 30 minutes, about 20 litres per capita per day); laundry and bathing not covered

quote: Segundo parâmetros internacionais, as cis­ ternas de consumo humano teriam garantido às famílias o acesso básico à água, nível mínimo a ser considerado no âmbito dos Objetivos de Desenvol­ vimento do Milênio (ODM). Nesse nível de acesso, a distância percorrida não ultrapassa um quilômetro, o tempo gasto não ultrapassa 30 minutos e o volume médio coletado é de 20 litros per capita por dia18. Nesse caso, o consumo humano e a higiene básica e dos alimentos são garantidos, mas há dificuldade de se garantir a lavagem de roupa e banho. (English: According to international parameters, human-consumption cisterns would have guaranteed families basic access to water, the minimum level considered under the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). At this level of access the distance travelled does not exceed one kilometre, the time spent does not exceed 30 minutes and the average volume collected is 20 litres per capita per day18. In this case human consumption and basic personal and food hygiene are guaranteed, but it is difficult to guarantee laundry and bathing.)

relationship.outcome_raw: in great multi-year droughts the domestic cistern runs dry and households fall back on water trucks (functional failure of storage, not structural damage)

context.note: implementer interview (Arsky 2019 dissertation); storage exhaustion under multi-year drought; cistern+water-truck described as a combined non-conventional supply system | process: retagged 2026-10-06 (Pete D3): storage running dry / benefit limited under drought is a benefit shortfall, not asset damage → nbs_effect, direction none (was asset_vulnerability, direction positive)

quote: Ocorre que, no entanto, mesmo com as cisternas, o carro-pipa continuou sendo uma realidade neces­ sária no semiárido e as pessoas continuam sujeitas à tentativa de uso político, porque a falta de água as coloca em uma situação muito vulnerável, como no caso das grandes secas plurianuais, explica a coordenadora local do MOC na Bahia: Então, imagina quando seca tudo. E a água da cis­ terna vai acabando. Como é que não dou um pote de água para meus bodes, minhas galinhas? Aí, o vereador chega lá e diz “não se preocupe, eu vou te dar um pipa”. Se, nesse momento, aquele vereador manda uma água para aquela família, ela vai ficar com um sentimento de gratidão [...]. Então, mas a água é um direito, e o direito não pode ser negociado. (Entrevista 5; Arsky 2019). (English: It happens, however, that even with the cisterns, the water truck continued to be a necessary reality in the semi-arid and people remain subject to attempts at political use, because the lack of water puts them in a very vulnerable situation, as in the case of the great multi-year droughts, explains the local MOC coordinator in Bahia: So, imagine when everything dries up. And the cistern water runs out. How can I not give a pot of water to my goats, my chickens? Then the councillor arrives and says 'don't worry, I'll give you a truckload'. If at that moment that councillor sends water to that family, she will feel gratitude [...]. But water is a right, and a right cannot be negotiated. (Interview 5; Arsky 2019).)
raw_name: cistern water runs out in multi-year droughts

relationship.outcome_raw: domestic cistern storage reduces dependence on water trucks and postpones or avoids extreme water-shortage situations (implementer perception + field observation)
relationship.direction_cue: adia ou até mesmo evita as situações limites

context.note: perception of programme implementers; no quantification

quote: Além disso, conferiu autonomia, porque a família beneficiada “consegue ficar sem depender do car­ ro-pipa. Ela tem independência, tem liberdade, ela não tem que vender o voto por causa do carro-pipa” (Entrevista 13, grifo meu; Arsky, 2019), explicou o presidente da ARCAS (BA). Foi muito fácil perceber, na observação direta da pesquisa de campo, como se apresentam as ca­ tegorias dignidade e autonomia. Resultado de um consistente processo de capacitação e conscien­ tização, existe hoje uma verdadeira cultura sobre o gerenciamento da água armazenada na cisterna, e a água de beber armazenada é tratada com zelo e cuidado. Essa reserva adicional, essa poupança, adia ou até mesmo evita as situações limites em que viviam essas famílias. (English: In addition, it conferred autonomy, because the benefiting family 'manages to go without depending on the water truck. It has independence, it has freedom, it doesn't have to sell its vote because of the water truck' (Interview 13; Arsky, 2019), explained the president of ARCAS (BA). It was very easy to perceive, in direct field observation, how the categories of dignity and autonomy present themselves. As a result of a consistent process of training and awareness-raising, there is today a true culture of managing the water stored in the cistern, and the stored drinking water is treated with zeal and care. This additional reserve, this saving, postpones or even avoids the extreme situations in which these families used to live.)
raw_name: autonomy from water truck; water reserve

relationship.outcome_raw: production ('second water') cistern keeps livestock watered while the household's clay tanks are dry and lets the family manage intermittent piped supply
relationship.direction_cue: It was good after this water

context.note: farmer interview, Fatima-BA; PROVISIONAL FAMILY: 'segunda agua' production technologies (cisterna calcadao / enxurrada, barreiro trincheira, subsurface dam; ground-surface runoff into storage) have no FAM sub-practice id; filed under water_harvesting__runoff_catchment pending a FAM decision; dry tanks not attributed by the speaker to a named drought (no hazard_type)

quote: A gente tinha dificuldade com a água, porque daqui da onde a gente mora, para as roças, para os tanques, é bastante longe, e agora não, porque a gente já ganhou a cisterna com bomba, e a extensão já vem com o próprio projeto. [...] Foi bom depois dessa água. Até agora mesmo, os tanques de barro estão secos e os animais estão se abastecendo da cisterna. A gente até parou de plantar um pouco, porque estamos poupando para os animais. [...] Se não fosse ela [a água estocada na cisterna] não dava. Porque a água da EMBASA [Empresa Baiana de Águas e Saneamento] não dá, porque passa da taxa. E, também, nós nem teríamos como armazenar, porque a água vem de oito em oito dias, e nós aqui em cima somos o último a receber, então quando chega nossa vez, já é hora de acabar de novo [...]. A água que tá na cisterna é da chuva e ainda tem como segurar alguns meses. (English: We had difficulty with water, because from where we live to the fields, to the tanks, it is quite far, and now not, because we got the cistern with a pump, and the extension comes with the project itself. [...] It was good after this water. Even right now, the clay tanks are dry and the animals are drinking from the cistern. We even stopped planting a bit, because we are saving it for the animals. [...] If it weren't for it [the water stored in the cistern] it wouldn't be possible. Because the EMBASA [Bahia water and sanitation company] water isn't enough, because it exceeds the fee. And also we wouldn't even have a way to store it, because the water comes every eight days, and up here we are the last to receive it, so when our turn comes it is already time for it to end again [...]. The water in the cistern is from the rain and can still hold out for some months. (Interview 15; Arsky, 2019).)

quote: tre estas tecnologias, o uso da irrigação de salvação tem reduzido os riscos da exploração agrícola em anos cuja precipitação pluviométrica é irregular, proporcionando até duas colheitas em anos considerados normais de chuvas. Segundo Porto et al. (1983), no Semi-Árido brasi- leiro, três em cada dez anos são considerados normais com relação à quantidade e à distribuição das chuvas. Define-se a irrigação de salvação como a lâmina de água aplicada à cul- tura nos veranicos que comumente ocorrem durante o período chuvoso na região Nordeste, de forma a não permitir que a cultura sofra estresse hídrico e, em alguns casos, morra. No Semi-Árido brasileiro, após as pri- meiras chuvas, é comum ocorrerem períodos de 20 a 30 dias sem novas chuvas, comprometendo seriamente a germinação e outras fases de de- senvolvimento das culturas. (English: [Am]ong these technologies, supplemental (salvation) irrigation has reduced the risks of farming in years with irregular rainfall, allowing up to two harvests in years considered normal. According to Porto et al. (1983), in the Brazilian semi-arid three in every ten years are considered normal in rainfall quantity and distribution. Salvation irrigation is defined as the depth of water applied to the crop during the dry spells (veranicos) that commonly occur during the rainy season in the Northeast, so as not to let the crop suffer water stress and, in some cases, die. In the Brazilian semi-arid, after the first rains, periods of 20 to 30 days without new rain are common, seriously compromising germination and other crop development phases.)

quote: Quanto ao uso, as barragens foram distribuídas em duas classificações: • 94 barragens ativas: aquelas que já foram utilizadas pela comunidade ao menos uma vez após a sua cons- trução; • 57 barragens inativas: nunca foram utilizadas pela comunidade após a sua construção. Estas se dividem em dois grupos: • 20 barragens inativas por motivo associado à popula- ção: são aquelas que estão em bom estado técnico, que têm acumulado água de boa qualidade, mas nunca fo- ram utilizadas pela comunidade por motivos diversos, discutidos a seguir; • 37 inativas por motivo técnico: barragens em que foram detectados preliminarmente problemas técnicos que impossibilitaram o uso pela comunidade. These divide into two groups: 20 dams inactive for population-related reasons: in good technical condition, accumulating good-quality water, but never used by the community for various reasons discussed below; 37 inactive for technical reasons: dams in which technical problems that prevented use were detected. relationship.outcome_raw: construction and siting failures of subsurface dams traced to lack of technical follow-up

context.note: co-authored by World Bank water staff (Baltar, Azevedo); OPERATIONAL RISK: technical-assistance capacity; construction-quality failure (no VONT id for construction quality); PROVISIONAL FAMILY: subsurface dam (barragem subterranea) has no FAM sub-practice id; filed under water_harvesting__runoff_catchment pending a FAM decision

quote: Problemas construtivos - Os principais problemas cons- trutivos detectados em algumas das barragens subterrâneas foram: • Erro de locação: local impróprio por apresentar bacia de contribuição pequena, e assim baixa capacidade de retenção de água; • Escavação insuficiente, sem alcançar a rocha no fundo da aluvião; • Problema com a lona na hora de sua colocação, sem alcançar o leito rochoso, permitindo fuga por baixo; • Solos com baixo nível de infiltração; • Poço com baixa permeabilidade, dificultando a entra- da de água; • Barragens construídas em solos salinizáveis. Esses problemas ocorreram em diferentes locais, em decorrência quase sempre da falta de acompanhamento técnico adequado. (English: Construction problems - The main construction problems detected in some of the subsurface dams were: siting error (improper site with a small contributing basin and so low water-retention capacity); insufficient excavation not reaching bedrock; problems with the plastic sheet during placement, not reaching bedrock and allowing leakage underneath; soils with low infiltration; well with low permeability hindering water entry; dams built in salinisable soils. These problems occurred in different places, almost always as a result of lack of adequate technical follow-up.)
raw_name: construction and siting failures of subsurface dams traced to lack of technical follow-up

The CTI is calculated as [100 × ln (α/tan (β))] where 
100 is used to convert the value to an integer, α = ((flow accumulation +1) × pixel area 
(m2)), and β = slope (radians) (Beven and Kirkby, 1979).
selection_justification:
In general, lower slope areas with sufficient overland runoff will collect water resulting in 
conditions with a greater potential to support wetlands.

relationship.direction: poorly and very poorly drained soils (longest, deepest saturation/inundation) indicate potential to support perennial wetlands; better-drained classes do not

quote:
From the drainage classifications, poorly and very poorly drained soils are the 
most frequent, longest, and most deeply saturated or inundated of the soil drainage classes 
and thus should be considered an indicator of potential to support perennial types of 
wetlands.
raw_name: SSURGO/STATSGO2 drainage class (poorly + very poorly drained, PVP)

relationship.unit: percent of soil map unit poorly or very poorly drained (PVP)
relationship.direction: at or above the PVP break point the soil represents the saturation and inundation duration needed for perennial wetlands; below it soils are more likely somewhat poorly drained and suit non-perennial wetland types, particularly in lower topographic positions — not an absolute exclusion

quote:
Therefore, we selected cells 
having a PVP of 80% as a break point for further analyses. As a secondary evaluation, we 
compared our PVP soil drainage grid to a soil grid having ≥50% hydric conditions. The two 
were in agreement 85% of the time, suggesting that our greater than 80% PVP soil grid 
adequately represented both the saturation and inundation duration necessary to support 
perennial wetlands. Grid cells with less than 80% PVP soils would likely include somewhat 
poorly drained conditions, resulting in moderate saturation and inundation durations that 
would more successfully support non-perennial types of wetlands, particularly when located 
in lower topographic positions (Tiner, 1999).
raw_name: percent poorly + very poorly drained soil per cell (PVP) break point
attribution: Horvath et al. 2017; PVP grid cross-checked against hydric-soil grid

relationship.direction: joint soil-drainage × topographic-wetness classification of potential wetland area; poorly drained soil can compensate for low CTI (low class) and vice versa (moderate class)

quote:
After defining the initial CTI threshold and the appropriate break points for PVP 
percentages, we combined the CTI and PVP layers into a single index layer of categorical 
classes of PWA: 1) high (CTI values ≥ 550 combined with 80–100% PVP of the summed 
soil components), 2) moderate (CTI values ≥ 550 combined with 1–79% PVP), 3) low (80–
100% PVP with CTI values ≤ 550), and 4) none (0% PVP or CTI values < 550 and < 80% 
PVP).
raw_name: Potential Wetland Area (PWA) classes combining PVP soils and CTI
attribution: Horvath et al. 2017 (EPA EnviroAtlas PWA layer)

relationship.direction: agricultural land (pasture/hay and cultivated crops) is the restorable target; developed land and large water bodies are excluded (impervious, commercially valuable, hydrology not restorable); natural covers are not targeted because they would not need extensive restoration — not because they are unsuitable

quote:
To create the PRW-Ag layer, we combined the PWA classes with LULC classes from the 
2006 NLCD. LULC classes that were unlikely to be selected for wetland restoration, such as 
developed lands or large water bodies, were excluded from the selection. While wetland 
restoration can occur and provide benefits within other land use classes, such as open or low 
intensity development sites, these developed classes are also more likely to contain 
unsuitable land cover such as impervious surfaces and may also be more likely to be 
commercially valuable for other uses. In such cases, buffers may be a more suitable 
alternative to offset impacts to streams. It was assumed that natural land covers, such as 
forest, grassland, and existing wetlands, would not require extensive restoration. We, 
therefore, focused on agricultural land (pasture/hay [land cover code = 81] and cultivated 
crops [land cover code = 82]) in combination with the PWA classes.
raw_name: NLCD 2006 land cover filter for potentially restorable wetlands on agricultural land (PRW-Ag)
justification_quote:
Wetland restoration is more likely on certain landscapes (e.g., agriculture) than others 
due to the lack of substantive infrastructure and the potential for the restoration of hydrology;

relationship.direction: suitability declines with slope; above the maximum the cell is not suitable for wetland creation/restoration (authors note the cap is a local design choice — wetlands can occur on steeper slopes in New Zealand)

quote:
Slope was the simplest derivative, since low slope angles are more suitable
for wetlands than steeper slopes. However, in New Zealand, wetlands can also occur on steeper
slopes. Therefore, in the current study, we deﬁned the maximum suitable slope for wetland as 3◦.
Smaller slopes were assigned a higher suitability for wetland development.
raw_name: maximum suitable slope for wetland (LiDAR DEM, 1 m)
attribution: Uuemaa et al. 2018 — GIS-MCA criterion (equal-weight linear sum of four criteria)
justification_quote:
topography, since a wetland area needs to be generally ﬂat,
but natural landforms, such as swales and gullies, can facilitate wetland construction [8];

relationship.direction: monotonic increasing — higher TWI, higher wetland suitability; used only as one criterion because TWI alone was insufficient
relationship.scale: TWI deciles within the catchment rescaled 0 to 1 (catchment-relative, not a transferable threshold)

quote:
Higher TWI values indicate higher soil moisture content and
also a higher suitability for wetland. TWI has been used effectively to predict soil moisture and has
also been tested for identifying wetlands by several authors [23,40]. However, TWI alone did not
provide sufﬁcient results. Therefore, we used TWI only as one parameter. TWI was calculated using
SAGA GIS [41]. Values of TWI were divided into deciles and assigned values from 0 to 1 to create
a suitability map.
raw_name: topographic wetness index (SAGA GIS) decile suitability
attribution: Uuemaa et al. 2018 — GIS-MCA criterion

relationship.direction: suitability decreases with distance from the (virtual) stream network and is zero beyond the maximum distance; closer to higher-order streams is better and the suitable band is wider along higher-order streams

quote:
We created distance maps with a maximum distance of 125 m from the streams, and converted them
into suitability maps with each pixel having values from 0 to 1. The closer a site is to a higher-order
stream, the higher its suitability as a wetland site. In addition, the suitable area around higher-order
streams was wider than around the lower-order streams.
raw_name: distance to streams (Strahler-order weighted) for in-stream wetlands
observed_dataset: virtual stream network from LiDAR DEM flow accumulation
attribution: Uuemaa et al. 2018 — in-stream wetland design only (off-stream options not considered)
justification_quote:
Therefore, the potential wetland sites in our analysis occurred along the streams or drainage
ditches, and there is a higher probability for suitable wetland sites to exist along the higher-order
streams.

relationship.direction: a wetland with too small a contributing area is ineffective at reducing pollutant loads; sites below the minimum contributing area are not delineated

quote:
The contributing area (i.e., the area that contributes water to the wetland) is an important criterion,
since wetlands with a too-small contributing area may be ineffective for decreasing pollutant
loads. (Here, we will focus on nitrogen pollution, but the same approach applies to most other
pollutants.) The minimum area we chose for this study was 50 ha.
raw_name: minimum contributing (drainage) area for a created wetland
attribution: Uuemaa et al. 2018 — effectiveness criterion for nutrient-interception wetlands

relationship.direction: suitability rises with distance from infrastructure (roads, farmsteads, other structures) and is full at the outer buffer — the wetland is created by flooding, so infrastructure must not be flooded (a physical-footprint constraint, not market access)

quote:
We applied multiple 10-m buffers up to a distance of 100 m
from the infrastructure. The buffer values were converted into a suitability map in which distances
from the road were assigned values starting from 0 m (beside the road) and ending with 1 at a distance
of 100 m from the road.
raw_name: distance to infrastructure (roads, farmsteads) to avoid flooding it
observed_dataset: NZ topographic map roads + orthophoto-classified infrastructure

avoided

End of Project Target

hectares of cultivated peat bog. Dokudovskoe  peatland rewetted (950 ha).

2.2.2. Forest and Tree Planting (Afforestation)
Afforestation involves transitioning agricultural land from row crop or pasture pro-
duction to forest lands, either actively managed for forest products or as a restoration
activity. Agroforestry practices also fall into this category and integrate tree production
with traditional row crop agricultural operations and livestock husbandry. Agroforestry
practices may increase income for farmers, particularly on sites with poor soil [42]. Suitable
sites for forest and tree planting were determined to have low-productivity soils, owned by
a single entity, and consisted of at least ﬁve acres (2 ha) in area (Figure 6).

Air temperature was lowered by up to 6°C at midday under compared to outside the canopy 
of F. albida (Figure 4.3c). Temperature reached 36oC and was highly variable in the open field, 
while it reached a maximum of 29oC and fluctuated less under the canopy. Temperature 
exceeded 28oC, for about six hours day-1 (i.e., from 10:00-16:00 GMT) in the open fields and 
for less than two hours (i.e., from 12:300-14:300 GMT) for under the canopy. For close to three

tree crowns than in open fields (P<0.001).

relationship.outcome_raw: maize hybrid grain yield, SR + Zaï + OM + NPK + Urea vs control (ploughing + NPK + urea), Houndé (letters a vs b)

context.region: Houndé district, Hauts-Bassins, North-Sudan savanna agro-ecological zone
context.practice_as_described: Stone rows fixed on contour lines (30-50 m apart) combined with zaï pits (micro basins dug in quincunx, earth crescent upstream to capture runoff), plus 5 t/ha organic fertilizer (cow dung and crop residues) + NPK (14-23-14) + urea
context.note: control = farmers' practice: oxen ploughing and application of mineral fertilizer (NPK + urea). Full-fertility arm vs control: both arms receive NPK + urea, so the contrast is SWC structures + 5 t/ha organic manure (not separated in the design).  Site rainfall 2014: 981 mm (10-yr mean 926 mm), less than Péni; authors attribute the larger Houndé response to greater water-stress severity. On-farm randomized block design, farmers as replicates; 2014 season; significance from Newman-Keuls letters (same letter = not different at 5%).

context.region: Péni district, Hauts-Bassins, South-Sudan savanna agro-ecological zone
context.practice_as_described: Grass strips + zaï pits, and earth bunds on contour lines + contour ploughing, each combined with organic and/or mineral fertilization options
context.note: Results for the SWC-technology comparison at Péni are stated as not shown in the paper.  Site rainfall 2014: 1488 mm (10-yr mean 1084 mm); authors state water was not limiting at Péni. On-farm randomized block design, farmers as replicates; 2014 season; significance from Newman-Keuls letters (same letter = not different at 5%).

quote:
In 2014 at Péni, soil and water conservation 
(SWC) practices did not have significant differences for 
maize grain and straw yields. Whereas at Houndé, there 
were significant differences between SWC practices for 
maize grain yields. This can be due to the difference in 
rainfall characteristics between the two sites. During the 
year 2014, the site of Houndé received less rainfall than 
Péni. Water was not a limiting factor at Péni, so that SWC 
practices did not induced significant improvement in 
maize yields.
raw_name: SWC effect on maize yield at Péni: null (water not limiting)

quote: Relationship between site elevation (cm above mean sea level) and flooding frequency (days per month) for each month of the year. Green colour coding shows elevations that are optimal for planting, and red indicates areas where careful site assessment is needed before deciding to plant. The brighter the red, the greater the need for site assessment. Elevations above 200 cm (2 m) and below mean sea level may be unsuitable for planting mangroves. Flooding frequency (days flooded per month) is based on tidal records from Ganh Hao tide station for the period 2010 to 2013. Note that the flooding frequency refers to the lower end (marked) of each elevation range, and the number of days flooded decreases with increasing elevation within each elevation band.
